title: dispatch-jitter-kernel-silos-apr-2026
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a focused Nsight Systems + CUDA Graphs session investigating a pattern we saw in production: intermittent SM sparsity (many SMs near-idle) during steady throughput windows, which correlates with 95th/99th tail spikes. Goal was to deconvolve whether the root cause is host-side dispatch jitter, stream/graph reification costs, or GPU-side wake/scheduling behavior.

Experiment setup (small repro):
- Model: small-decoder (12B-ish) quantized int8 runtime build on current main branch.
- Workload: steady 50 requests/s synthetic traces, input lengths 64/512 mix to exercise attention kernels.
- Deployment: single A100-80GB, driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.2.
- Instrumentation: nvtx ranges around request lifecycle, nsys timeline capture:
  nsys profile --capture-range nvtx --output dispatch-jitter-run1 nsys-report --sample=none --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --stop-on-range-end
- Also captured cudaGraph creation/launch traces with NVTX markers.

What we observed (high level):
- Two distinct micro-patterns in the timeline:
  1) Steady microbatches where kernels chain tightly across SMs (expected) and throughput looks flat.
  2) Short (~200-900us) windows where a large fraction of SMs show <20% active time and a small number of kernels dominate on a subset of SMs. These windows map to host-side gaps between kernel launches.
- The host gaps are not constant: they show jitter up to ~1.2ms in some traces.
- CUDA Graph launches reduce, but do not eliminate, these gaps. Graph capture time and instantiation overhead shifts the pattern (graphed runs have fewer but larger gaps).

Detailed timeline notes:
- NVTX marker: REQUEST_START -> prepare_batches -> KERNEL_x -> KERNEL_y -> KERNEL_z -> REQUEST_END. During bad windows, see: REQUEST_START, prepare_batches, (host idle ~700us), KERNEL_x fire only on 8 out of 80 SMs, then later KERNEL_x repeats with another subset of SMs.
- These align with thread wakeups on the host side: the worker thread that pushes kernels appears to be preempted or blocked by short syscalls (epoll/poll wake queuing), causing kernel emission to be serialized in micro-silos.
- Nsight timeline shows persistent GPU-side queues with small FIFO gaps; the HW command processor is waiting for more work and does not aggressively re-distribute work to idle SMs until new kernels arrive.

Metric snippets (sampled off nsys):
- Avg SM occupancy (good windows): 63%
- Avg SM occupancy (bad windows): 18%
- Tail latency delta (p99) correlated with bad windows: +11ms over baseline
- Kernel launch window variance (host inter-launch): sigma ~ 220us (ungraphed), peaks 1.2ms

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Host dispatch jitter due to Python GIL/GC/asker event loop scheduling -> serialized kernel submissions leading to SM micro-silos.
2) Interaction between our batching thread and OS scheduler: worker threads are not pinning to cores, occasionally preempted by higher-priority system work.
3) CUDA Graphs reduce CPU work but graphite instantiation or replay synchronization introduces periodic larger gaps; Graph replay sometimes hits small synchronization fences in our wrapper causing batched launches to be fragmented.
4) GPU-side hardware scheduling: some sequences of kernels are not amenable to SM-resident balancing (e.g., kernels with divergent occupancy or block distribution), causing fragmentation even if host dispatch is prompt.

Repro steps to isolate host jitter vs GPU-side:
- Run synthetic microbenchmark that submits the exact same kernel chain from a tight C++ spinloop pinned to a dedicated CPU core (no Python, no syscalls). Compare occupancy and tail.
- Run under rr/strace to detect unexpected syscalls in worker thread.
- Force NOP kernels between stages to observe if issuing kernels earlier collapses silos.
- Test cudaGraph capture-mode vs explicit launches and measure inter-kernel timestamps.

Short experiments run so far:
- C++ pinned producer reduces inter-launch sigma to ~35us and removes most SM-silhouette windows. p99 latency regresses to near baseline. -> strong evidence host-side.
- Launching via cudaGraphCapture/Instantiate/Launch: reduces CPU load by ~18% but added an occasional ~800us synchronization point when we recreate graphs for batch-shape changes.
- Adding a micro-batching prefetcher that coalesces two requests into a single larger submission reduced observed SM sparsity but increased average latency by ~1.5ms (tradeoff).

Artifacts and quick links:
- Repro repo: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/bench/dispatch-jitter-repro
- PR with thread pinning experiment: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482
- Jira: JIRA-ENG-1872 (Dispatch jitter -> tail spikes)

Open questions / TODOs:
- Are there kernel-level changes we can make to improve cross-SM balancing for short kernels? (Diego to try increasing blocks-per-SM packing for attention kernels).
- Should we introduce an in-process real-time scheduling hint for worker threads (chrt/SCHED_FIFO) or explicitly pin threads to avoid preemption? Evaluate CPU-affinity changes (Owen).
- Investigate whether the CUDA driver exposes per-stream asynchronous copy prescheduling options that would make kernel emission independent of host emission timing.
- Evaluate enabling the low-latency CPU governance knob (cgroups/isolcpus) on our Dedicated instances to see if that stabilizes inter-launch jitter.

Action plan (next 2 weeks):
1) Diego: run kernel packing experiments + report whether occupancy improves without changing host code (ETA 2026-04-12).
2) Owen: run production-like stress with worker threads pinned to isolated cores; measure p99 and nsys traces (ETA 2026-04-09).
3) Maya: prototype light-weight coalescing layer that merges near-simultaneous submissions into a single CUDA Graph if input shapes match; measure latency tail impact (ETA 2026-04-16).
4) If host pinning reduces variance, bake CPU-affinity as a deploy knob in runtime agent and run limited canary on Dedicated region.

Notes to self:
- Keep NVTX markers minimal but descriptive. Avoid nested spans that make capture range splitting painful.
- When analyzing nsys reports, sort by "GPU Active" time and look for small clusters of kernel execution separated by host idle gaps.
- Remember to correlate with SLO metric pipeline (metric ids in JIRA ticket).

Conclusion (tentative):
Early evidence points to host-side dispatch jitter as the dominant contributor to transient SM sparsity and tail latency spikes. CUDA Graphs are useful but not a silver bullet — they reduce average CPU overhead but can introduce periodic synchronization costs when graphs are recreated or when capture boundaries align poorly with dynamic batch shapes. The most promising immediate mitigation is worker thread CPU-affinity + lighter-weight coalescing at the runtime layer.

Appendix (commands & capture knobs):
- nsys capture example used:
  nsys profile --capture-range nvtx --capture-range-end-on-exit true --output dispatch-jitter-run1 --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --sample=none --stats=true python -u -m bench.dispatch_repro
- nvprof is deprecated — prefer nsys + nvtx. Use --sample=none to keep timeline fidelity.
- NVTX tagging plan: REQUEST_START, PREPARE_BATCH, CUDAGRAPH_BEGIN, KERNEL_STAGE_1, KERNEL_STAGE_2, CUDAGRAPH_END, REQUEST_END

References and reading:
- CUDA Graph Best Practices (internal notes + NVIDIA docs)
- Nsight Systems timeline primer (internal cheat-sheet in /shared_drives/engineering/observability/)
